chunks: Muhammad ibn Abi Abdillah, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Asbat, from al-Husayn ibn Zayd, from Dorost ibn Abi Mansur, from one who narrated it to him, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:
Six things — the servants have no role in them: gnosis, and ignorance, and contentment, and anger, and sleep, and wakefulness.

key_terms.الرِّضَا: Rida — contentment, divine pleasure, inner satisfaction; a spiritual station in Sufi and Shia thought
key_terms.الْجَهْلُ: Jahl — ignorance; used here in its theological sense as the absence of divine ma'rifa, not merely lack of information
key_terms.الْغَضَبُ: Ghadab — anger; an emotional state whose underlying disposition is not fully under human control
key_terms.الْمَعْرِفَةُ: Ma'rifa — spiritual gnosis, direct recognition of God and divine realities; a higher form of knowledge beyond intellectual learning
key_terms.صُنْعٌ: Sun' — making, action, agency, craftsmanship; here meaning human agency or free participation

ai.seo_question: What are the six things that servants have no control over according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) declares that six fundamental states — spiritual gnosis (ma'rifa), ignorance (jahl), contentment (rida), anger (ghadab), sleep (nawm), and wakefulness (yaqaza) — lie entirely outside human agency and are bestowed directly by God. This teaching addresses a deep theological question about the relationship between divine sovereignty and human free will, asserting that these particular inner states are not products of human choice or effort but divine gifts or impositions. This hadith appears in the chapter on God's arguments upon His servants, suggesting it is meant to clarify the scope of human accountability.

en.hubeali:
Muhammad Bin Abu Abdullah, from Sahl Bin Ziyad, from Ali Bin Asbat, from Al Husayn Bin Zayd, from Dorost Bin Abu Mansour, from the one who narrated it, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having said: ‘
Six things, there isn’t a the servants to play a role with regards to these – The recognition, and the ignorance, and the pleasure, and the anger, and the sleep, and the waking up (from the sleep)’.
